vignette: A blood culture flag is positive; the Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters.
stem: Which is the most appropriate next test to begin identification?
explanation: Gram-positive cocci in clusters: the first branch test is catalase (Staphylococcus/Micrococcus are catalase-positive; Streptococcus is catalase-negative). Coagulase follows catalase to identify S. aureus.

rationales.A: Oxidase differentiates gram-negative rods (Pseudomonas vs Enterobacterales).
rationales.B: Correct: catalase separates staph from strep first.
rationales.C: Urease is used later (e.g., Proteus, Helicobacter).
rationales.D: Coagulase comes after catalase; it cannot separate staph from strep.

misconception: Order of testing matters: catalase before coagulase for gram-positive cocci.

vignette: A sputum Gram stain shows many squamous epithelial cells (>10 per low-power field) with mixed flora.

choices.text: Report the mixed flora and continue full workup
Reject/recall the specimen as contaminated by oropharyngeal flora
Report it as normal flora only
Treat it as a sterile-site specimen

explanation: Squamous epithelial cells >10/LPF indicate saliva contamination; the specimen does not represent the lower respiratory tract and should be recollected to avoid misleading results.

rationales.A: Continuing a workup on an invalid specimen wastes resources and misleads therapy.
rationales.B: Correct: standard sputum acceptability criteria require rejection/recollection.
rationales.C: Reporting 'normal flora' masks the quality problem.
rationales.D: Sputum is not a sterile-site specimen; its quality must be assessed first.

misconception: Specimen quality criteria are as examinable as organism identification.
